questions.stem: Use the lecture's values: interstitial pressure −3 mmHg, interstitial oncotic 8 mmHg, venous-end capillary pressure 10 mmHg. A patient with liver failure has plasma oncotic pressure 18 mmHg. What is the net pressure at the venous end?
questions.explanation: Outward 10 + 3 + 8 = 21; inward 18; net 3 mmHg outward, so the venous end now filters. A: The normal venous value (plasma oncotic 28). B: Omits interstitial oncotic pressure. C: Treats the −3 mmHg interstitial pressure as an inward force. E: Uses the arterial-end capillary pressure (30 mmHg).

questions.stem: Which structural feature makes hepatic sinusoids the most permeable type of capillary?
questions.explanation: Discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillaries, e.g. liver, have fenestrae plus large gaps. A: Fenestrated capillaries (small intestine, exocrine glands). C: Continuous capillaries (skeletal muscle). D: Blood–brain barrier capillaries. E: The glycocalyx is a barrier, not a source of permeability.

questions.stem: A solute has a reflection coefficient of 0 across a capillary wall. What does this mean?

options.A: It is fully reflected and exerts its full osmotic force
options.B: It crosses as easily as water and exerts no osmotic force
options.C: It crosses faster than water does
options.D: It crosses only by active transport
options.E: It is held back by the glycocalyx

questions.explanation: σ = 0: the solute leaks through as rapidly as water, so its gradient produces no fluid flow. A: That is σ = 1 (no leakage). C: That is a negative σ (rare). D: σ says nothing about active transport. E: Being held back means σ near 1.

questions.stem: According to the revised (Landis–Pappenheimer) model, what happens when capillary pressure is held steadily below plasma oncotic pressure?

options.A: Sustained absorption, as classic Starling predicts
options.B: Increased filtration at the venous end
options.C: No sustained absorption; absorption is only transient

questions.explanation: Real measurements show absorption only transiently, after abrupt drops in capillary pressure, not at steady state, because fluid exchange occurs with the subglycocalyx space. A: The classic prediction that real data contradict. B: Low pressure doesn't raise filtration. D: Lymph flow continues. E: Not predicted by the model.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with right heart failure has bilateral pitting ankle edema. Serum albumin is normal. Which Starling force change is mainly responsible?
questions.explanation: In cardiac failure, raised pressure at the venous end of the capillary favors filtration over absorption. B: Albumin is normal. C: There's no inflammation or toxin. D: Lymphatics are intact. E: Lower interstitial oncotic pressure would oppose edema.

questions.stem: Shortly after losing 1.5 L of blood, a trauma patient's hematocrit begins to fall before any IV fluids are given. Why?

options.E: Absorption of interstitial fluid into plasma

questions.explanation: A sudden drop in capillary pressure (shock) favors absorption of interstitial fluid into capillaries, diluting the red cells. A: Filtration falls. B: Increased permeability would move fluid out of plasma. C: Marrow changes take days. D: Lymphatic obstruction causes edema, not plasma dilution.

questions.stem: After axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, a 52-year-old woman develops persistent arm edema. Which Starling change contributes most?
questions.explanation: Normally more fluid is filtered than absorbed, and lymphatics return the excess fluid and protein. With lymphatic blockage, protein accumulates in the interstitium, raising interstitial oncotic pressure. B: Plasma proteins are normal. C: Raised capillary pressure is heart failure. D: Reduced permeability would limit edema. E: The edematous interstitium becomes less negative, not more.
